content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to recast domain generalization as a convex game between domains. This work uses the supermodularity property of the convex game to formulate a regularization term, and rigorously demonstrates that the growth of domain diversity will enhance model generalization monotonically. This work also utilizes a sample filter to eliminate the bad samples of harmful information to generalization performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

S1. This work is well-motivated, which focuses on exploring the diversity of source domains and model generalization. The idea of improving generalization with domain convex game to best utilize the rich information within input data is reasonable.

S2. The experimental results and ablation study on extensive benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

Weaknesses:

W1: Overall, the novelty and technique contributions of the proposed framework are limited. Improving the generalization ability via domain augmentation and meta-learning has been largely explored, e.g., L2A-OT [1], Mixup [2], and MLDG [3].

W2: The paper does not discuss the computational complexity of the domain convex game training process.

W3: The authors are expected to propose some intuition on why the proposed method outperforms the L2A-OT, MixStyle presented in Table 3.

W4: The authors are expected to quantify how many augmented samples are almost distinguishable with source domains and thus encourage the diversified domain.

[1] Learning to Generate Novel Domains for Domain Generalization, ECCV 2020.

[2] Mixup: Beyond empirical risk minimization, ICLR 2018.

[3] Learning to Generalize: Meta-Learning for Domain Generalization, AAAI 2018.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces a method to address the problem of domain generalization(DG). They give a novel perspective to this problem based on  based on game theory. They cast the DG problem as a convex game between domains which makes each diversified domain contribute to the improvement on generalization. They also propose a regularization term based on the super modularity of the convex game and claim that it encourages the model to better utilize the information from diversified domains. Further, they give method for filtering samples that hurt generalization. They conduct extensive experiments on real datasets and find that their method does better than other baseline methods for domain generalization.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The paper brings an interesting a novel perspective based on convex games to the problem of domain generalization.  They give a training method with regularization term motivated from the convex game's super-modularity and a filtering step to exclude bad samples that could hamper generalization. The proposed method is evaluated on benchmark datasets for domain generalization and the comparison against the baselines is pretty comprehensive. Moreover, the numbers suggest that their method outperforms the baselines on most of the benchmarks. 

Weaknesses/Questions:
1. The description of method in sections 3.2 and 3.3 is somewhat unclear. It seems like test data is getting used to figure out which domains (or samples) are useful or not. Could you please clarify this ? May be have a separate algorithm clearly describing all the steps. 

2. Game theoretic aspects are not quite illustrated. Seems like the super-modularity is sufficient to explain the setup and game theoretic details are not needed ( or utilized).   

3. It is hard to judge the empirical effectiveness without seeing the spread of the reported metric.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Most parts of the papers are clearly written and the contributions seem novel and the experiments look to to be reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a novel method for domain generalization and shows it's benefit empirically. Details of the method can be made more explicit and clear. I have a few questions/concerns listed above. Theoretical analysis and more insights into the game theoretic aspects could improve the paper.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the relation between domain diversity and OOD performance on domain generalization: will increased domain diversity always benefit OOD generalization? The proposed DCG (domain convex game) shows that diversity does not always ensure good OOD performance, but can sometimes hurt the performance due to noisy and redundant samples. DCG takes inspiration from convex game that tries to solve such a game using convex game theory. They used Fourier to construct augmented samples. Then, split the training data as meta-train and meta-test sets, where meta-learning can be performed. To further filter out the noisy or redundant samples, authors used the existing gradient score as the confidence. Experiments are conducted on PACS, Office-Home, and mini-DomainNet.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength

1. The problem formulation is good. It is novel and interesting to study the relation between domain diversity and OOD performance. Such motivation is clear and strong.
2. This paper is well-written, easy to follow, and clear.
3. Experimental results are good.

### Weakness

1. Introducing convex game theory is good. But I feel that this paper may overclaim in terms of formulation using convex game. The only difference from existing meta-learning-based DG is that they also consider augmentation parts: $S \bigcup T$ and $S \bigcap T$, and the associated eq. (7). In fact, removing the convex game does not hurt the methodology since splitting the training domains into meta-train and meta-test sets is common in DG.
2. How to deal with the situation that $S \bigcap T=\emptyset$ in the algorithm?
3. The sample filter part is not novel since it's just a direct adoption of existing work.
4. With regards to figure 1, it is not clear which augmentation approach is used to get these results. Additionally, authors did not try all possible augmentation approaches to claim that diversity does not necessarily guarantee increased OOD performance. It also depends on what can be viewed as "augmentation". Interpolation (mixup) and Fourier transform are all good augmentation techniques, but GAN/VAE-based approaches are also augmentation approaches. How to measure their contribution to OOD performance remains unanswered in this paper.
5. Although several methods are involved in experiments, there should be extensive comparison with augmentation-based approaches, which this paper only covers a few. For instance, Mixup is only compared in mini-DomainNet, which it shows very strong performance according to the reviewer's knowledge. Authors should also compare GAN/VAE based augmentation approaches.
6. There is no theory to guarantee that this method will converge, which to our knowledge, is that MAML (MLDG) is not stable to train.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:** Most of the paper is clear and well-written.

**Quality:** This paper is of medium to high quality of all my reviewed ICLR submissions.

**Novelty:** The idea of introducing convex game theory is novel. But I doubt the necessity of its introduction since we can also do the same thing without the theory.

**Reproducibility:** Source code is provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: To sum up, this paper is interesting in its discovery of convex game to domain generalization. However, it still has the above flaws, especially the sufficient motivation and technical relation to the theory.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a regularization approach for domain generalization which ensures that the optimization of a model proceeds through a trajectory where augmenting it with further training samples (where each training sample is a new domain) improves performance as we keep adding more domains. That is, given a current parameter vector \theta, we check the benefit of adding a new domain to the current domain set, and ensure that the marginal contributions of adding the new domains are constant (not decreasing). This is the key novelty of the paper, in addition to which the paper also adds other tricks such as rejection of low-quality samples using some heuristics. Overall the combination of the approach and other heuristics leads to state of the art leave-one-out OOD domain generalization performance on PACS, Office Home and Domain Net.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Positives
+ The paper tackles an important problem, namely that often adding additional domains / augmentations hurts performance and that improvements are not often monotonic
+ Understanding why this happens/ rectifying this remains an interesting and open problem. The paper does a good job of exposing this issue.

Negatives
- Why would optimization not converge to a solution where the marginal gains of adding domains all become a constant (0) which means we still satisfy the Eqn. 7 but dont actually get the desired effect?
- There is a lot of verbose exposition of domain convex games and other topics which dont necessarily seem central to the paper. In my opinion, the paper can be written much more simply, and it is not clear what the domain convex game exposition adds to the paper beyond a lot of notations. This is more of a case especially since the actual objective does not even utilize the supermodular property. 
- More algorithmic and implementation level details need to be provided. A number of things remain unclear regarding implementation from a reading of the paper as submitted. For example, 1) what does it mean to take the gradient of L_{sm} with respect to a datapoint x in the set of augmented and source domains? As far as I understand we minimize L_{sm} with respect to the parameters of the loss function \theta to find an initialization from which using S, T, S U T and S \int T satisfies some constraints when using the respective losses. When computing gradient of Eqn. 3 with respect to ‘x” are we also considering that the current “\theta” depends on x in the dataset or are we just looking at the part of the gradient that is contributed to by \calF? 
- When training what does one step of gradient update of the entire model with respect to \theta look like? That is, it would really help to show a training algorithm that corresponds to Eqn. 10. Otherwise it is really hard to get a sense of how one might implement this method. Also, it needs to be clarified how S, T are chosen at each training step. 

Minor points:
- It would help to give an intuition of what the “ideal” curves in the plot of Fig. 1 represent and what they mean, and how they are computed. Without that it is hard to get an intuition for what is going on.
- S \in 2^m is wrong notation
- How reasonable is it to call D_aug with one data point that is augmented as a “domain”?
- Ablations on \alpha
- How much does sample rejection contribute to performance?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper can improve on the clarity of the exposition. Specifically an algorithm for training that dicusses how S and T are chosen (Eqn. 3) and how the overall update of the parameters \theta looks would be very useful. Please see negatives above more more clarity issues.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a method that works really well in practice in leave one out validation domain generalization settings. Conceptual motivation of the work is also strong. The demerits are the somewhat loose connection to convexity of domains which seems to add a lot of jargon without adding much in insight, and lack of clarity of certain aspects. Overall, with improvements in these aspects the paper might be a good addition to the conference program.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.
